question: What percentage of weight loss from pre-pregnancy weight helps nurses identify hyperemesis gravidarum?

options.A: Loss of exactly 2 percent of body weight
options.B: Loss of more than 5 percent of body weight
options.C: Loss of up to 1 percent of body weight
options.D: Loss of 1 to 3 percent of body weight

explanation: Dropping more than 5% of her original body weight is a key sign that a mom-to-be has moved past normal morning sickness into severe hyperemesis. You've got this! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h1)

question: How does hyperemesis gravidarum differ from normal pregnancy morning sickness?

options.A: It only occurs during the final trimester of pregnancy
options.B: It causes severe, unstoppable vomiting leading to dehydration and weight loss
options.C: It has no effect on the overall fluid balance of the body
options.D: It usually resolves completely within the first four weeks

explanation: While normal morning sickness is manageable, hyperemesis involves nonstop vomiting that drains the body's fluids and nutrition. Great job keeping the clinical differences clear! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h1)

question: Which hormone is most strongly linked to the severe nausea of early pregnancy?
explanation: Rapidly rising levels of human chorionic gonadotropin peak in the first trimester and strongly correlate with intense nausea and vomiting. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h2)

question: Which pregnant patient has the highest risk of developing hyperemesis gravidarum?

options.A: A woman in her third trimester experiencing mild heartburn
options.B: A primigravida with low levels of estrogen and progesterone
options.C: A woman carrying twins with a family history of the condition
options.D: An older adult woman with low blood pressure

explanation: Carrying multiples pushes hormone levels sky-high, and family genes play a big role too. Spotting these risk factors makes you a fab nurse! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h2)

question: What finding in a pregnant patient's urine points to prolonged vomiting and starvation?
explanation: When the body can't keep food down, it starts burning its own fat for fuel. This breakdown leaves behind ketones in the urine—a classic sign of prolonged vomiting! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h3)

question: A pregnant patient with hyperemesis has low potassium and high blood pH. What is happening?
explanation: Pumping out stomach acid through continuous vomiting strips the body of hydrogen ions, causing blood pH to rise. That's metabolic alkalosis in action—keep smashing those lab values! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h3)

question: Why is a severe lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine) a major worry in hyperemesis?

options.A: It directly causes sudden gestational diabetes in the second trimester
options.B: It triggers immediate placental abruption and severe bleeding
options.C: It can lead to serious neurological issues like Wernicke's encephalopathy
options.D: It stops the production of amniotic fluid completely

explanation: Starvation and vomiting deplete vitamin B1, which can trigger confusion and nerve issues known as Wernicke's encephalopathy. Knowing this helps you protect your patients early! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a common fetal complication linked to untreated hyperemesis?
explanation: Heart defects happen during early structural development, whereas hyperemesis baby issues are usually about poor nutrition and low birth weight. You're mastering neonatal risks! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h4)

question: What is the best daily nursing action to track fluid loss in a hyperemesis patient?

options.A: Checking the patient's blood pressure twice a shift
options.C: Asking the patient how many times she vomited
options.D: Weighing the patient at the same time each day

explanation: Daily weights don't lie! They give you an exact mathematical picture of how much fluid and tissue mass the patient is losing. Simple and super effective. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h5)

question: Why might doctors order a thyroid test for a patient with severe hyperemesis?

options.A: It helps check the exact gestational age of the fetus
options.B: Thyroid failure is the primary cause of all pregnancy vomiting
options.C: High levels of hCG can temporarily stimulate the thyroid gland
options.D: Thyroid medication is always used to cure morning sickness

explanation: Because hCG hormone looks a bit like thyroid-stimulating hormone, sky-high pregnancy hormones can trick the thyroid into working overtime. Brilliant clinical insight! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h5)

question: What is the primary medical goal when admitting a patient with hyperemesis gravidarum?

options.A: Feeding the patient a heavy high-protein meal right away
options.B: Starting immediate surgical options to empty the uterus
options.C: Discharging the patient with herbal teas and rest
options.D: Correcting fluid and electrolyte imbalances with IV fluids

explanation: Before anything else, we must rehydrate and restore lost electrolytes to keep vital organs safe. You're thinking like a real ward nurse! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h6)

question: Why is vitamin B1 added to an admitted pregnant patient's intravenous fluid bag?

options.A: To prevent severe brain disorders like Wernicke's encephalopathy
options.B: To increase the baby's birth weight within twenty-four hours
options.C: To lower the patient's blood pressure back to normal
options.D: To instantly stop the uterus from having early contractions

explanation: Thiamine protects the brain from the nasty effects of prolonged vomiting and malnutrition. Ward protocols made easy! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h6)

question: Why is mouth care an essential part of the nursing care plan for hyperemesis?

options.A: Good mouth care cures the underlying hormonal imbalances
options.B: Stomach acid from vomiting damages teeth and leaves a bad taste
options.C: Brushing teeth stops the stomach from contracting
options.D: It prevents the patient from swallowing her own saliva

explanation: Vomiting coats the mouth in harsh stomach acids that eat away at tooth enamel. Regular mouth care keeps her teeth safe and her breath fresh. Spot on! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h7)

question: Which nursing action helps reduce nausea triggers in a hospital room?

options.A: Opening the window wide during meal service times
options.B: Playing loud music to distract the patient from her symptoms
options.C: Keeping the room free from strong food odors and bright lights
options.D: Encouraging the patient to eat three large meals daily

explanation: Strong smells and glaring lights can easily set off a vomiting wave in a sensitive pregnant mom. A calm, scent-free room works wonders! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h7)

question: Why should a recovering hyperemesis patient avoid drinking lots of fluid during meals?

options.A: It permanently ruins the function of the kidneys
options.B: It stretches the stomach quickly and can trigger vomiting
options.C: It washes away all the digestive enzymes in the mouth
options.D: It causes severe cramping in the lower extremities

explanation: Chugging water alongside food overfills the stomach too fast, which is an express ticket right back to vomiting. Small sips separate from meals are best! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h8)

question: What tip should a nurse give a pregnant woman to help prevent severe morning nausea?

options.A: Drink a large glass of orange juice immediately upon waking up
options.B: Skip breakfast entirely until the afternoon hours arrive
options.C: Keep plain crackers near the bed and eat a small amount before getting up
options.D: Exercise vigorously for twenty minutes before eating breakfast

explanation: Nibbling a dry cracker before getting out of bed lifts morning blood sugar and settles an empty stomach. Classic nursing advice that really helps patients! [learn more](GNS226_U2_T016#GNS226_U2_T016_h8)
